analysis.one_liner: Makes online small-dollar lenders register with the CFPB and obey state interest-rate caps.
analysis.headline: A bill backed by 19 senators to make online payday lenders follow state rate caps and stop draining bank accounts died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Lending Act targeted predatory small-dollar online lending. It would have required lenders of loans up to $5,000 to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, forced internet and phone lenders to follow the interest-rate caps of the state where the borrower lives, and stopped lenders from pulling money from bank accounts through checks and transfers the borrower never authorized. It also banned overdraft fees on prepaid cards and barred websites from collecting and selling borrowers' bank details unless they actually make the loan.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who use payday and other small-dollar loans, most often low- and middle-income workers living paycheck to paycheck. They would gain the right to stop automatic electronic repayments, protection from unauthorized remotely created checks draining their bank accounts, the interest-rate and fee limits of their own state applied to online lenders, and no more overdraft fees on prepaid accounts. Their bank details would also be safer from resale by lead-generation websites.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payday borrowers and prepaid card users

how_it_helps.text: Lets a borrower cut off automatic electronic repayments: any agreement to repay a small-dollar loan by electronic transfer would be treated like a preauthorized transfer, which comes with a right to stop payment.

Blocks a common collection tactic: remotely created checks — checks drawn on a borrower's account that the borrower never signed — could only be issued by someone the borrower designated in writing to their bank, and the borrower could revoke that designation at any time.

Closes the rate-evasion loophole for online loans: internet, phone, mail, and email small-dollar loans, and small-dollar loans made by national banks, would have to follow the annual-percentage-rate and fee rules of the state where the consumer lives, rather than the rules of a lender-friendly state.

Requires anyone making, brokering, or arranging small-dollar consumer loans (up to $5,000, with the threshold adjusted for inflation and raisable by the Bureau) to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before lending.
Prohibits overdraft fees on prepaid accounts — a fee that falls on people who use prepaid cards instead of bank accounts — and lets the Bureau block related fees by rule.

Bars lead generators from facilitating the distribution of sensitive financial information (Social Security numbers, bank account and routing numbers, access codes) for small-dollar loans unless they are the ones directly making the loan, and requires them to disclose who they are and where they can be served legal papers.

Directs the Government Accountability Office to study access to capital on tribal reservations and how small-dollar lending has affected economic opportunity for tribal members, with a report to the relevant committees.

analysis.who_pays: Payday and online installment lenders, who would face federal registration, state rate caps on their internet business, and new limits on collecting payments; lead-generation websites that profit from selling loan applicants' bank details; and banks that earn overdraft fees on prepaid accounts or use partnerships to originate high-rate loans nationally. Borrowers who currently rely on high-cost short-term credit could face fewer options if lenders exit rather than register and comply.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not set its own rate cap — it applies whatever each state allows. In the states with no interest-rate ceiling on small loans, online lenders could still lawfully charge triple-digit rates, so protections would vary sharply by where a borrower lives.

Extending state rate caps to online lending and adding federal registration would make some high-cost lenders exit the market or stop lending in certain states, reducing the availability of short-term credit for borrowers who use it; the industry's standard objection is that these borrowers would be pushed toward unlicensed lenders or missed bills. The bill attempts to counter abuse with registration and lead-generation rules rather than a replacement source of small-dollar credit.

The bill leans heavily on the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write implementing rules within one year and to define key terms (the loan-size threshold, prepaid accounts, covered payment orders), so its real-world effect would depend on how aggressively the Bureau of the day writes and enforces those rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are concrete and aimed at documented abuse: unauthorized remotely created checks draining accounts, stop-payment rights, state rate caps applied to online loans, and an end to overdraft fees on prepaid cards. The honest cost is that some borrowers who use high-cost short-term credit would have fewer lawful lenders to turn to, since lenders that cannot profit under their home state's rules may simply stop lending there — which is partly the bill's intent. The bill leaves the biggest gaps (states with no rate caps, reliance on future CFPB rulemaking) unresolved. On balance it shifts risk from borrowers to lenders, at the price of reduced access to the most expensive credit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing, a markup, or a vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the SAFE Lending Act on March 5, 2019, joined by 18 cosponsors — 17 Democrats and one independent — including Senators Harris, Sanders, Warren-adjacent progressives like Markey and Blumenthal, and Durbin. No Republican signed on.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, the committee with jurisdiction over consumer credit law.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action. The bill sat in committee until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and died there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online payday and small-dollar lenders and the lead-generation industry are better off, because the existing rules — internet lenders picking a lender-friendly state's law, unchecked electronic account withdrawals, and resale of borrowers' bank details — stayed in place. Borrowers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online payday lenders and lead generators

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors were Democrats or independents and none of the Senate's 53 Republicans cosponsored; the Republican-run Banking Committee then took no action, so the fight followed party lines even though no roll-call was ever held.

industries.note: The bill forces these lenders to register with the CFPB, apply the borrower's home-state rate caps to internet and phone loans, and stop seizing payments through unauthorized remotely created checks and unstoppable transfers. Their business model of lending online under the rules of whichever state is most permissive would largely close.

These companies collect loan applicants' Social Security and bank account numbers and sell them to lenders; the bill makes it illegal to move that data for a small-dollar loan unless you are the one directly making the loan, eliminating their role in this market.

National banks making small-dollar loans would have to follow the consumer's home-state rate rules, closing partnership channels used to export high-rate lending nationwide, and issuers of prepaid accounts could no longer charge overdraft fees on them.

Some online lenders operate under tribal sovereignty claims to avoid state caps; the bill applies the borrower's home-state rules to all internet small-dollar loans and, rather than exempting tribal lenders, orders a GAO study of lending's effect on tribal members' economic opportunity.
